2. The rule arises in the following circumstances:—The opposite parties as plaintiffs have instituted a Suit being Title Suit No 288 of 1967 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca for a declaration of their raiyati right in respect of 16 annas share in the suit property and also for a declaration that the notice No. 536 (18) V-2/67 dated 15-6-67 issued by the Member, Board of Revenue and all subsequent actions taken by him are illegal, void and without jurisdiction. The plaint case is that the suit land was the Khas land of the Bhowal Estate and on the prayer of one Torah Ali and 16 others the Khas land was settled with them by the Bhowal Estate at annual dental of Taka 1500 in the year 1344 B.S. and since their settlement they were in possession demarcating the boundaries. Some of the plaintiffs are transferors from the Original settlement holders. During the State Acquisition Settlement Operation the suit land was illegally recorded in the name of the defendant petitioner. Whereupon the plaintiff-opposite parties filed a petition under section 143 of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act for correction of the record and thereafter the Sub divisional Manager, Sadar South, on the recommendation of the Circle Inspector and Tahsilder submitted a proposal to the A.D C. (Revenue, for recognition of the tenancy-right of the puff opposite parties and the A. D.C. (Rev.) recognized their said right and realised rent from them. Thereafter the Board of Revenue passed an order cancelling the recognition of the tenancy right of the plffs. and declaring that the aid land was the Khas land of the Bhowal Estate and after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it became the Khas land of the Government In the meantime the entire land was acquired under the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 by the Govt. and compensation was paid to some of the plaintiff ; But the order of the Board of Revenue having cast some cloud on their title, they have instituted the above mentioned suit. Thereafter, at a certain stage of the suit the plaint was amended. After the amendment of the plaint the defendant-petitioner filed an additional written statement; subsequently defendant petitioner wanted to make some amendments in paragraph 10 of the additional written statement. Accordingly prayer was made on a verified petition for amendments to be made in paragraph 10 of the additional written statement. But the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the prayer for amendment on the ground that the amendment, if allowed, would prejudice the plaintiff-opposite parties. Thereafter the present rule was obtained by the defdt.- petitioner. 

 8. Mr. Ranadhir Sen has argued that by the amendment, if allowed, no prejudice will be caused to the plaintiff-opposite parties. Rather the amendment will help determination of the real question in controversy between the parties. The plaintiff opposite parties claim their tenancy right in the suit land on the basis of settlement of their vendors from the Bhowal Estate while the case of the defendant-petitioner is that the land was Khas land of the Bhowal Estate and after the acquisition under the Acquisition and deviancy Act the suit land became the Khas land of the Government as it was not found retainable by the ex-landlord. Mr. Sen further states that at certain stage the land was acquired under the Emergency Requisition Act and some of the plaintiffs got compensation but from this payment of compensation it cannot be said that their ownership was admitted in the land. The compensation might have been paid on the basis of possession. But inadvertently it was stated in para 10 of written statement that provisional compensation was paid to the owners of the land. It seems Mr. Ranadhir Sen has argued rightly that the statement that provisional compensation was paid to the owners of the land was made through inadvertence and that it was nothing but a bonfire mistake which is now sought to be deleted by the proposed amendment. In the khatian also the possession of some of the plaintiffs appears to have been recorded with the remark ‘No title to the land’. In this view of the matter Mr. Ranadhir Sen, we think, has rightly argued that the amendment, if allowed, will not cause any prejudice to any claim of the plaintiff opposite parties.
